title: One Month at Johns Hopkins Hospital
paragraphs: From March to April 2023, I was allowed to train for four weeks in pediatric hematology at Johns Hopkins Hospital (hereafter abbreviated JHH). Here I would like to introduce the clerkship, centring on a typical day.

Pediatric hematology is divided mainly into ward work in the morning and outpatient work in the afternoon. There are always about 5 to 6 patients admitted to pediatric hematology, and I was in charge of one of them. In the morning I received a handover from the doctor on the night shift, checked the chart early in the morning, and greeted and examined the patient before rounds. In the first week I made the rounds together with a resident and learned what to check in the chart and, in addition, what to check in the physical examination. For the following three weeks, I came to round on my own patient by myself, thinking about the patient's condition and changes and the day's treatment. I put all of this together and, before the gathering, created in the chart the basis for the presentation at the morning rounds.

The rounds are made by one attending, one fellow, two residents and myself. Before entering the patient's room, the resident in charge or I give a presentation, reporting on the course of the admission, the current situation and the future treatment policy. At this point, not only reporting the current status but also proposing future treatment, we received advice from the fellow and the attending and their approval. After discussing all of this, we picked out the points we wanted to confirm with the patient and entered the room.

In pediatric hematology at JHH, rounds took more than 30 minutes per patient, and it was very challenging to first ease the child's tension and then explain the condition carefully in a way that even a child could understand. Furthermore, since it was necessary to explain not only to the patient but also to the guardians, I talked with my patient and their family while imitating the doctors' rounds. When I ran into the language barrier at times, the doctors standing behind me kindly supported me. I always felt reassured, and my motivation rose to do my best the next day. After rounds, I received feedback from the attending. Including strengths and points for improvement, they sometimes also gave mini-lectures.

Everyone's rounds end at about noon, and after this the outpatient clinic begins. The resident doctors, including me, take the lead and hear from the outpatients. I summarised the information obtained there and presented to the attending. After repeated discussion for each patient and once the policy was decided, we returned to the examination room together with the attending. After observing the attending's practice, I received feedback and a lecture.

That was a typical day. As you may have sensed, I think it is a medical setting rich in independence and education. In this one-month clerkship, I experienced ways of relating to patients and practising medicine different from Japan. Although I was surprised on the first day of the clerkship to be entrusted with the interviews of two outpatients, the joy of receiving mini-lectures during rounds and the atmosphere of thorough discussion of treatment policy regardless of years since graduation were also experiences I would not trade for anything. I sincerely thank the doctors of the International Collaboration Office and the doctors at JHH who gave me this valuable opportunity to study abroad. And, believing that I will make use of this experience and connect it to my future life as a doctor, I lay down my pen here.
